lead: A real aircraft part rarely sees a steady stress: a gust, a landing or a pressurisation cycle pushes it up and down. Every fluctuating stress splits into a steady mean part and a to-and-fro alternating part. The stress ratio fixes the shape of the cycle. A constant-life diagram then folds both parts into a single factor of safety against fatigue.
prereq: You need: fatigue: S-N curve and endurance limit for the endurance limit and the S-N curve, and failure theories: maximum principal stress and strain for combining stresses at a point.

blocks.text: One fatigue cycle runs between a maximum stress σ<sub>max</sub> and a minimum stress σ<sub>min</sub>, both in MPa, tension positive. Split it about its midpoint.

blocks.where: σ<sub>m</sub> is the mean stress, the steady part (MPa); σ<sub>a</sub> is the alternating stress, the half-swing about the mean (MPa); the range is σ<sub>r</sub> = σ<sub>max</sub> − σ<sub>min</sub> = 2σ<sub>a</sub>.

blocks.text: The stress ratio R = σ<sub>min</sub>/σ<sub>max</sub> fixes the shape of the cycle. The amplitude ratio A = σ<sub>a</sub>/σ<sub>m</sub> carries the same information, A = (1 − R)/(1 + R); it is infinite at R = −1, where σ<sub>m</sub> = 0. The value of R tells you which cycle you have.

items: R = −1: fully reversed, σm = 0 and σmax = −σmin — the rotating-bending test of fatigue: S-N curve and endurance limit.
R = 0: zero to maximum (pulsating tension), σ<sub>min</sub> = 0, so σ<sub>m</sub> = σ<sub>a</sub> = σ<sub>max</sub>/2.
R = 1: steady load, σ<sub>a</sub> = 0; fatigue does not arise.

blocks.text: Plot σ<sub>m</sub> across and σ<sub>a</sub> up. Each point is one cycle. For a chosen life a curve separates safe cycles from failing ones. For infinite life it meets the vertical axis at the endurance limit S<sub>e</sub>, where σ<sub>m</sub> = 0; for a finite life it meets it at the fatigue strength for that life. It meets the horizontal axis at a static strength, where σ<sub>a</sub> = 0. Only the part with σ<sub>a</sub> ≥ 0 has meaning.

Goodman: σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>u</sub> = 1;  Gerber: σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + (σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>u</sub>)² = 1;  Soderberg: σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>y</sub> = 1
blocks.where: S<sub>e</sub> is the endurance limit (MPa), S<sub>u</sub> the ultimate tensile strength (MPa), S<sub>y</sub> the yield strength (MPa).

blocks.text: Goodman is a straight line from S<sub>e</sub> to S<sub>u</sub> and the usual conservative choice. Gerber is a parabola through the same two points and follows ductile test data better. Soderberg runs from S<sub>e</sub> to S<sub>y</sub> and is the most conservative. The Langer line σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> = S<sub>y</sub> is plain first-cycle yielding: when the peak stress σ<sub>max</sub> = σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> reaches S<sub>y</sub>, the part yields at once, whatever its fatigue life.

The factor of safety n scales both stresses until the load point touches the curve. Put nσ<sub>m</sub> and nσ<sub>a</sub> into the line: Goodman gives 1/n = σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>u</sub>, Soderberg gives 1/n = σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>y</sub>. Gerber gives a quadratic in n; take the positive root.

figure.caption: Constant-life lines for S<sub>e</sub> = 400, S<sub>u</sub> = 800 and S<sub>y</sub> = 600 MPa. The fitting of the worked example, σ<sub>m</sub> = 100 and σ<sub>a</sub> = 200 MPa, lies inside all of them. Scaling it along its load line reaches the Goodman line at (160, 320), so n = 1.60; Soderberg gives 1.50 and Gerber 1.89. The Langer line marks first-cycle yield.

spec.aria: Alternating stress against mean stress. A straight Goodman line from 400 on the vertical axis to 800 on the horizontal axis, a steeper Soderberg line to 600, a dashed Gerber parabola bulging above Goodman, and a dotted Langer yield line from 600 to 600. The load point 100, 200 sits inside, and a dotted ray from the origin through it meets the Goodman line at 160, 320, labelled n equals 1.60.

examples.question: A steel aircraft fitting sees σ<sub>max</sub> = 300 MPa and σ<sub>min</sub> = −100 MPa. Take S<sub>e</sub> = 400 MPa, S<sub>u</sub> = 800 MPa and S<sub>y</sub> = 600 MPa. Find σ<sub>m</sub>, σ<sub>a</sub>, R and A, the factor of safety by Goodman, Soderberg and Gerber, and check first-cycle yielding.
steps: Yield check: σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> = 200 + 100 = 300 MPa, below S<sub>y</sub> = 600 MPa, so the first cycle does not yield.
examples.answer: σ<sub>m</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>a</sub> = 200 MPa, R = −0.33, A = 2.0; n = 1.60 by Goodman, 1.50 by Soderberg and 1.89 by Gerber, and the fitting does not yield on the first cycle.
examples.check:
smax, smin = 300.0, -100.0
Se, Su, Sy = 400.0, 800.0, 600.0
sm = (smax + smin)/2
sa = (smax - smin)/2
R = smin/smax
A = sa/sm
n<sub>good</sub> = 1/(sa/Se + sm/Su)
n<sub>sod</sub> = 1/(sa/Se + sm/Sy)
a = (sm/Su)**2
b = sa/Se
n<sub>ger</sub> = (-b + (b*b + 4*a)**0.5)/(2*a)
for v in (sm, sa, R, A, n<sub>good</sub>, n<sub>sod</sub>, n<sub>ger</sub>):
    print(round(v, 2))

traps: Dividing S<sub>e</sub> by σ<sub>a</sub> while a tensile mean stress acts. The mean part also spends life; use σ<sub>a</sub>/S<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub>/S<sub>u</sub>. The shortcut n = S<sub>e</sub>/σ<sub>a</sub> holds only at R = −1.
Writing R = σ<sub>max</sub>/σ<sub>min</sub>. It is R = σ<sub>min</sub>/σ<sub>max</sub>, and compression keeps its sign: −100/300 = −0.33, not +0.33.
Putting S<sub>u</sub> where S<sub>y</sub> belongs. The Goodman line ends at S<sub>u</sub>, Soderberg at S<sub>y</sub>, and the Langer line sits at S<sub>y</sub>.
Checking the fatigue line only. A large mean stress yields the part on cycle one, so always test σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> against S<sub>y</sub>.

Forgetting compressive yield. With a compressive mean stress the most compressive stress, σ<sub>min</sub> = σ<sub>m</sub> − σ<sub>a</sub>, can yield the part on the first cycle, so check |σ<sub>min</sub>| against the compressive yield strength too.

quiz.q: Define σ<sub>m</sub> and σ<sub>a</sub> in terms of σ<sub>max</sub> and σ<sub>min</sub>.
quiz.a: σ<sub>m</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> + σ<sub>min</sub>)/2, the steady part; σ<sub>a</sub> = (σ<sub>max</sub> − σ<sub>min</sub>)/2, the half-swing about the mean.

quiz.q: Give the stress ratio R for (a) fully reversed, (b) zero to maximum, (c) steady loading.
Why does the Gerber curve sit above the Goodman line between σ<sub>m</sub> = 0 and σ<sub>m</sub> = S<sub>u</sub>?
quiz.a: Both join S<sub>e</sub> at σ<sub>m</sub> = 0 to S<sub>u</sub> at σ<sub>a</sub> = 0. Gerber is a concave-down parabola, so at any intermediate mean stress it allows a larger alternating stress than the straight Goodman chord. Goodman is the conservative bound.

quiz.q: A cycle runs from σ<sub>min</sub> = 50 MPa to σ<sub>max</sub> = 250 MPa. Find σ<sub>m</sub>, σ<sub>a</sub>, R and A.
S<sub>e</sub> = 350 MPa, S<sub>u</sub> = 700 MPa, σ<sub>m</sub> = 140 MPa, σ<sub>a</sub> = 200 MPa. Find n by Goodman and state whether the part is safe.
quiz.a: 1/n = 200/350 + 140/700 = 0.571 + 0.200 = 0.771, so n = 1.30. The point lies inside the line, so it is safe.

quiz.q: A part passes the Goodman check but yields on the first overload. How is that possible?
quiz.a: For ductile steel S<sub>u</sub> exceeds S<sub>y</sub>, so near the σ<sub>a</sub> = 0 end Goodman allows σ<sub>max</sub> = σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> above S<sub>y</sub>. The fatigue line protects against many cycles, not against first-cycle yield; the Langer line σ<sub>a</sub> + σ<sub>m</sub> = S<sub>y</sub> must be checked as well.

beyond: Not for the exam. A real airframe sees a random load spectrum, not one tidy cycle; rainflow counting breaks the spectrum into blocks and Miner's rule adds up their damage. Damage-tolerance design instead accepts a growing crack and inspects it before it reaches critical length. Search for rainflow counting, Miner's rule and fatigue damage tolerance in aircraft structures.
